claims.text: A high-temperature solutionizing step followed by controlled cooling or aging can steer phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
As-cast or homogenized Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys may have mixed or multiphase microstructures containing undesired secondary phases.
Controlled cooling or aging adjusts the kinetics of phase nucleation and growth.
The thermal treatment should be performed under an inert atmosphere.
Solution treatment should occur above a critical temperature at which diffusional homogenization occurs.
The evolution and stabilization of FCC, BCC, and intermetallic phases mediate the alloy's mechanical and thermal properties.
High temperature enhances diffusion in the alloy.
Enhanced high-temperature diffusion allows the alloy to attain thermodynamic homogeneity.
Controlled cooling or aging changes local diffusion kinetics and thermodynamic driving forces.
Changes in diffusion kinetics and thermodynamic driving forces influence the nucleation and growth of different phases.
Controlled thermal processing can optimize the FCC-to-BCC balance and suppress unwanted phase transformations.
The treatment will produce a tailored microstructure with improved control over phase fractions.
Improved control over phase fractions will produce more consistent mechanical properties and enhanced performance relative to untreated samples.
Without controlled thermal treatment, the alloy is expected to have a less uniform phase distribution and less predictable or detrimental phase transformations.
Treatment efficacy depends on precise control of temperature, duration, and cooling rate.
Treatment efficacy may be sensitive to small compositional variations.
Controlling phase evolution through thermal processing is a well-established general concept.
Optimal solutionizing temperatures, cooling rates, and aging times for Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs require experimental fine-tuning.
